summary: Discusses the signals that on-path network elements can observe from transport protocols, contrasting implicit signals with explicit ones. For example, the clear-text messages of TCP's state machine are often used by network devices, while encrypted transports expose less. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Transport messages can reveal information to firewalls, translators, and other devices along a network path. This RFC recommends encryption by default and explicit, integrity-protected signals only when endpoints want path devices to act on them.

questions: implicit vs explicit signals in transport protocols
how does encryption affect firewalls and nat
subtitle: What on-path network devices can infer from transport protocols and how explicit signals should work.

tldr.problem: Network devices have inferred connection information from visible transport messages, but encryption hides those messages from the path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes implicit path signals, compares options for replacing them, and gives principles for explicit signaling when endpoints want path elements to use it.
tldr.outcome: The IAB recommends confidential operation by default, avoiding implicit signals, and using explicit signals only when their originator intends path elements to use them.

today: RFC 8558 is an Informational IAB document published in April 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC records the IAB's recommendation and says that signaling mechanisms remained under discussion.

sections.title: Implicit Signals from Transport Messages
sections.content:
An implicit signal is information that a network element infers by examining transport messages, even though those messages were designed for the endpoints. TCP's cleartext connection messages are one example. A firewall may use them to allow return traffic after an internal host starts a connection and later remove that allowance when the connection ends.

When a transport encrypts fields used for its state management, path elements cannot read those signals. The behavior then depends on the device's configuration and defaults. The RFC notes that losing the signals may be intentional when endpoints want confidential communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices can learn about a connection by reading transport messages. Encryption hides those messages, so the devices must use their own defaults instead.

sections.title: Information Visible to the Path
sections.content:
Path elements may infer a flow's identity from packet headers, whether two hosts can reach each other, and whether a connection is likely to continue. Load-balancing devices may use this information to keep a flow on one path. Firewalls and translators may also reserve state for a flow.

Devices can infer resource needs and measure path latency or reliability by observing timestamps, packet timing, sequence numbers, gaps, or retransmissions. The RFC says this list is illustrative, not exhaustive, and these are inferences rather than signals explicitly intended for the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Visible packet details can reveal which flow a packet belongs to and whether traffic is delayed or lost. Devices may also use those details to reserve resources or keep packets on one route.

sections.title: Options for Replacing Implicit Signals
sections.content:
The RFC considers four options: do not restore the signals; provide them at the network layer; define signals separately for each transport; or create signals shared by several transports. Each choice has trade-offs. Without signals, some devices may keep flow state for less time, so traffic may need to keep bindings alive.

Network-layer signaling could use IPv6 hop-by-hop headers, though the RFC says deployability needs more examination. Transport-specific signals risk becoming tied to one transport. Shared signals across transports may reduce the chance that the first transport to adopt them determines how the mechanism is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers can leave signals out, put them at the network layer, define them per transport, or share them across transports. The RFC describes trade-offs and does not prescribe one signaling mechanism.

sections.title: The IAB's Recommendation
sections.content:
The IAB urges protocol designers to support confidential operation by default, encourages implementations to encrypt by default, and urges firewall administrators to permit encrypted traffic. It recommends avoiding implicit signals and replacing one with an explicit signal only when the signal's originator intends path elements to use it.

Information for endpoint state machines should be confidential and integrity-protected. Any information exposed to the path should be intended for path use and integrity-protected, and should be separate from endpoint state signals. Intermediate elements should not add visible signals that identify a user, origin node, or origin network. The RFC notes that path elements generally cannot verify integrity without shared keys or trust points.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep endpoint control information private by default. If endpoints want network devices to use a signal, expose it separately and protect it against changes.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
A path element controlled by an attacker can drop, delay, or mishandle packets based on visible signals. Observers may also use signal patterns to characterize flows or identify communicating nodes. Adding visible information can reduce privacy if it can be linked to a user or device.

An endpoint may falsify an explicit path signal without changing the peer's view of an encrypted flow, and an on-path device may not detect the difference. The RFC advises protocol designers to consider how false signals affect operation and deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Path-visible information can help a device act on traffic, but an attacker could misuse it or use it to identify a user. Designers must consider how devices and endpoints handle false signals.
